the main library building will open at nine a.m. instead of ten, and will remain open until midnight on both Saturday and Sunday.
The twenty-four hour study wing on the third floor will continue to operate around the clock, but
the entrance to that wing will be relocated to the east side of the building while the front staircase undergoes routine maintenance.
Students using the study wing after eleven p.m. will be required to show a current university ID at the relocated entrance.
Group study rooms on the second floor may now be reserved online up to seventy-two hours in advance, and a small number of rooms will be held for walk-in use during peak evening hours.

We are also reminding everyone that the quiet conversation policy remains in effect throughout all reading areas, and food is still restricted to the first floor café. Thank you for your cooperation, and have a productive weekend.

source: Today I want to talk about a phenomenon that has reshaped how scholars think about early cities in Mesopotamia.
For decades, archaeologists assumed that large urban centers appeared rather suddenly around 3500 BCE, propelled mainly by the rise of writing and centralized administration.
Recent survey work in the northern alluvial plain, however, suggests a more gradual transition.
Excavations at smaller sites show that long before monumental architecture emerged, communities were already coordinating irrigation, storage, and craft specialization across considerable distances.
So the traditional boundary between a complex chiefdom and a true state may be much fuzzier than we once believed.

One team, for instance, documented clay sealing practices at a hamlet that had previously been written off as marginal. Those seals imply administrative behavior usually attributed to palace economies.
This kind of evidence is pushing researchers to treat the preliterate period as socially sophisticated in its own right, rather than as a mere prelude to the urban revolution.
The takeaway, then, is that the standard textbook story probably underestimates how much organization existed before the first cities declared themselves on the landscape.
